summary_paragraph: A 52-year-old female with systemic lupus erythematosus, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, and a history of cardiomyopathy was admitted for intermittent substernal chest pressure radiating to the back, worse with movement, and associated with nausea. The pain began after her morning dialysis and recurred the previous evening. Initial evaluation showed stable vital signs, new T-wave inversions in V5-V6 on EKG, and a mildly elevated troponin of 0.08, which remained stable on repeat testing. Chest X-ray revealed mild pulmonary vascular congestion without acute findings. The pain was reproducible on chest wall palpation, and no signs of acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, or pericarditis were found. After ruling out cardiac causes with serial troponins and clinical assessment, the pain was attributed to a musculoskeletal etiology, possibly related to recent heavy lifting and her known left rotator cuff tear. She was managed with her home hydromorphone regimen, avoided NSAIDs due to ESRD, and discharged home the following day with no medication changes and instructions to follow up with her primary and specialty providers.
problems: Chronic glomerulonephritis in diseases classified elsewhere
Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage V or end stage renal disease
